title: Given K sorted linked lists, merge them into one sorted linked list and return its head.
shortTitle: Merge K Sorted Lists: min-heap of K heads
keyPoints: Put the K list heads into a min-heap; repeatedly poll the smallest, append it, and push its successor.
The heap holds at most K elements, so each push and poll is O(log K), giving O(N log K) total time.
This exploits the per-list sorted property by comparing only K fronts at a time instead of all N elements.
A dummy head node simplifies appending by avoiding a special case for the first element.
The naive concatenate-and-sort approach is O(N log N) and ignores the existing sorted order.
The divide-and-conquer pairwise merge alternative also achieves O(N log K) without a heap.
Space is O(K) for the heap; the output list reuses existing nodes.

s1_definition.oneliner: Put the K list heads in a min-heap; repeatedly pop the smallest, append it, and push its next, giving a sorted merge in O(N log K).
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Min-heap of K fronts** – holds one candidate from each list, ordered by value, enabling O(log K) extraction of the global minimum.
- **Poll and push** – extract the smallest node, append to output, push that node's successor into the heap.
- **O(N log K) time** – each of the N nodes is pushed and polled once at O(log K) cost.
- **O(K) space** – the heap never exceeds K entries.
- **Dummy head** – a sentinel node simplifies appending logic by avoiding the special case for the first output node.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine K sorted queues of pending settlements at the National Bank of India, each already ordered by time. To merge them into one master-ordered stream, you look only at the front of each queue, pick the earliest, move it to the master list, and advance that queue by one. A small priority board of K fronts tells you instantly which queue currently has the earliest item.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Min-Heap Merge of K Sorted Lists:

  List 1: 10 -> 30 -> 50
  List 2: 20 -> 40
  List 3: 15 -> 25 -> 60

  Heap (fronts): [10, 20, 15]

  Step 1: Poll 10, append, push 30  -> Heap: [15, 20, 30]
  Step 2: Poll 15, append, push 25  -> Heap: [20, 25, 30]
  Step 3: Poll 20, append, push 40  -> Heap: [25, 30, 40]
  Step 4: Poll 25, append, push 60  -> Heap: [30, 40, 60]
  Step 5: Poll 30, append, push 50  -> Heap: [40, 50, 60]
  Step 6: Poll 40, append, (no next) -> Heap: [50, 60]
  Step 7: Poll 50, append, (no next) -> Heap: [60]
  Step 8: Poll 60, append, (no next) -> Heap: []

  Output: 10 -> 15 -> 20 -> 25 -> 30 -> 40 -> 50 -> 60
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Merging K sorted lists into one sorted list is solved by putting one head from each list into a min-heap and repeatedly polling the smallest, appending it to the output, and pushing its successor. Because the heap always surfaces the global minimum among the K fronts, the output comes out in sorted order. Each node is pushed and polled exactly once at O(log K) cost, giving O(N log K) total time with O(K) space.

This beats the naive concatenate-and-sort approach of O(N log N) because it exploits the per-list sorted property, comparing only K fronts at a time. The pairwise divide-and-conquer merge is an equally efficient alternative at O(N log K) without a heap.

In a banking system at the National Bank of India, settlement events from K regional systems, each already sorted by timestamp, are merged into one globally ordered stream. The min-heap holds only K fronts in memory, producing the master order in a single pass without sorting the combined volume from scratch.

This algorithm is also exactly how external merge sort combines sorted runs from disk, which is the technique banks use for enormous transaction files that do not fit in memory.

Remember one sentence: put K list heads in a min-heap, repeatedly poll the smallest and push its successor, and the output comes out sorted in O(N log K) time.
